catalog_quote: As it is the case with many Tupian accent-languages, the stress in Awetí generally falls on the last syllable of the stem. [...] The general rule of stress in Awetí, that the last syllable of the stem carries the stress, is independent of the nasality or other segmental-structural features of the syllables, in particular of their vowel quality and their ‘weight’. This means that syllables with any vowel and with or without consonants in coda or onset position can carry stress. Stress is also independent of the word class. [...] The majority of suffixes, inflectional as well as derivational, do not change the stress position, which remains on the last syllable of the stem. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (defined by Drude as the syllable's capacity to carry sentence-level/syntactic accentuation) falls on the last syllable of the stem (root). Weight, vowel quality and word class are irrelevant. The domain is the stem, not the word: the great majority of inflectional suffixes (aspect -ju/-(z)oko, mood -(t)u/-aw, negation -(y)ka, case suffixes) and class-changing derivational suffixes leave stress on the stem-final syllable, so a suffixed word is typically not stressed word-finally. Stress shifts to the suffix only with the purposive -°apan, the progressive allomorph -°eju, and derivational suffixes that do not change word class (-'at, -ka, -(t)ukat, -tej, -tut, nominal tense -(p)ut, -(z)ã'jap). Awetí is not tonal, and Drude 2021 hypothesises that accent is not phonologically contrastive (no minimal pairs found); the main acoustic correlate is pitch (rising contour on the stressed syllable), not intensity or duration.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No general secondary-stress rule is stated. Drude 2011 (40), p. 21, labels the nominal negation suffix -e'ym as carrying 'secondary stress' while main stress stays on the stem; stative verbs with the progressive allomorph -eju have two stressable syllables (stem-final and suffix /e/), the choice varying with speaker, style and rhythm, and in isolation both often get high pitch (33), p. 19. Intensity is nearly uniform across syllables and Drude explicitly hesitates to postulate trochaic feet (p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate stress in: some 30 verb stems ending in a lenis consonant + /e/ (o-tige, o-mỹje; the /e/ analysed as a thematic morph); a few verbs in final unstressed -ã (o-kangã); a large group of animate/plant nouns ending in -yt (pyringyt, takanyt, nukakyt) versus regular final-stressed kujãkyt, ekyt, tywyt; a few other nouns (takarĩ, momati, momatsaza) and the pronoun ozoza (groupal suffix -za unstressed); adverbs in fused unstressed -wo/-pe/-ti/-ko (kype, ypytako); most postpositions in -o (ewizako, pywo, 'apo); the postposition kyty with varying stress; second-position particles (weti, wene, wian, zanu, tene, wezanu). Final sentential particles are clitics without stress. Stress-attracting suffixes as listed in the rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word form (phonological word); stress is treated as a lexical property of the stem-final syllable realised through syntactic (sentence) accentuation, so citation forms in isolation show it. Drude notes (fn. 21) that some Tupí-Guaraní descriptions posit a domain larger than the word; his acoustic study (secs. 6-8) used single word forms and carrier sentences. Language as a whole (ca. 150 speakers in 2011, ca. 300 per Drude 2021); no dialect qualification.
new_statements.identity_note: Awetí (awet1244) as spoken in the Upper Xingu villages (Mato Grosso); Drude worked with the community 1998-2010 (DOBES project). No separate dialects are distinguished; Drude 2011 mentions only one lexical 'dialectal variant' (takarĩ ~ takanyt). Glottolog lists Drude 2011 under a working title ('Word accent and its manifestation in Awetí', pp. 189-218, as cited in Drude 2019); the published paper is 'Stress in Awetí and its acoustic correlates', Amerindia 35: 7-40, as Drude 2021's own bibliography confirms.
